H1.text: You stand on a bathroom scale. You sink into a mattress. A car stays parked on a steep road.

H2.text: Each time, a surface is pushing back. And that push is not always what you think.

H3.text: Diya puts her pressure cooker on the kitchen scale. It reads three kilograms.

H4.text: Then she presses down on the lid. The scale jumps to four and a half! But the cooker did not get heavier.

H5.text: So what is the scale really measuring? The answer is the normal reaction.

P1.text: So what is the normal reaction?

P2.text: When a body presses on a surface, the surface pushes back. We call this push the normal reaction, N.

P3.text: Normal means perpendicular. N always points straight out of the surface, at ninety degrees to it.

P4.text: It is a contact force. Lift the body off, and N is gone.

P5.text: And a surface can only push. It can never pull.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A two kilogram box sits on a scale.

S2.text: Its weight, m g, is nineteen point six newtons. The scale pushes up with N, also nineteen point six.

S3.text: Now a hand presses down with ten newtons. The scale pushes back harder. N climbs to twenty nine point six.

S4.text: Now the hand lifts up with ten newtons. N drops to nine point six.

S5.text: On the graph, every newton of push adds one newton to N. So a scale shows N, not your mass.

S6.text: Next, tilt the scale into a ramp, and watch N.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze at thirty degrees.

S8.text: Split the weight in two. m g cos theta presses into the surface. m g sine theta points down the slope, and friction holds the box still.

S9.text: N only has to balance the part that presses in. So N is m g cos theta. About seventeen newtons.

S10.text: Let it run. At sixty degrees, N is half of m g. The steeper the ramp, the smaller N.

S11.text: Your turn. You press a book flat against a wall with fifteen newtons. It stays still. What is the normal reaction? Pause and decide.

S12.text: Fifteen newtons! The wall pushes back against your push. The weight points along the wall, not into it.

D1.text: Now let's write it down, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. The box does not sink in, and it does not jump off. So the forces perpendicular to the surface add up to zero.

D3.text: Step two. On a flat surface, N pushes up and m g pulls down. N minus m g is zero. So N equals m g.

D4.text: Step three. Push down with a force F. Now N must hold up m g plus F. N equals m g plus F.

D5.text: Step four. Pull up with F instead. Your pull does part of the job, so N equals m g minus F.

D6.text: Step five. On a ramp at angle theta, only m g cos theta presses in. So N equals m g cos theta.

T1.text: Remember this. N is the surface pushing back, and it is not always m g.

K1.text: Side by side. Push down on the box with ten newtons, and N grows.

K2.text: Pull up with ten newtons, and N shrinks. Same box, same weight, different N.

K3.text: Now you try. Pull the two kilogram box up with twenty five newtons. How hard does the scale push? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Zero! N can never go below zero. A surface can only push, so the box simply lifts off the scale.

W2.text: Diya's cooker is three kilograms. She presses the lid down with fifteen newtons. Find N, and the scale reading. g is nine point eight.

W3.text: The weight is three times nine point eight. That is twenty nine point four newtons.

W4.text: She pushes down, so N equals m g plus F. Twenty nine point four plus fifteen. Forty four point four newtons.

W5.text: A scale shows N divided by g. Forty four point four over nine point eight is about four point five three kilograms.

W6.text: That is the jump Diya saw. The cooker is still three kilograms. Only N changed.

X2.text: On a ramp, many students write N equals m g sine theta.

X3.text: Check it on flat ground, where theta is zero. Sine zero is zero, so N would vanish. Wrong! Cos zero is one, so N equals m g. It must be cos theta.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In free-body numericals: blocks on ramps, and blocks pushed or pulled at an angle.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A two kilogram block sits on a smooth ramp at thirty seven degrees, held still by a horizontal push. Sine thirty seven is point six, and g is ten. Find the normal reaction. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Twenty five newtons.

A2.text: Along the slope, F cos theta balances m g sine theta. So F is fifteen newtons.

A3.text: Into the surface, m g cos theta is sixteen newtons, and F sine theta is nine.

A4.text: N balances both: twenty five newtons. So N can be bigger than m g!

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why did the scale jump when Diya pressed the lid?

Y3.text: Two. Can a normal reaction ever pull a body?

Y4.text: Three. On a ramp, why is N equal to m g cos theta, and not m g sine theta?

N1.text: Next time: a rope lifts a bucket out of a well. Is the pull in the rope always the bucket's weight? We find out in tension.
